passage:
Dear Rukmini,
Something scary happened on the way back from iftar at Nani's on Thursday, and you're the only one who won't lecture me.
I was walking down our lane, texting Farah about Eid outfits. I was watching the road too, I swear, in little glances. Then the fruit-seller uncle yanked my arm so hard I dropped the phone. Right in front of my feet was the open drain pit the workers dug last week, with a red ribbon around it. A red ribbon! I must have looked at it five times.
Two steps later a cyclist rang his bell right at me. I hadn't seen him either.
My hands shook the whole way home. Now the phone stays in my bag until I'm inside our gate.
Write back soon,
Zainab

qa.q: What was around the open drain pit?
qa.a: A red ribbon.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after the fruit-seller uncle's yank, and why?
qa.a: Zainab felt shaken and scared, hands trembling all the way home, after seeing that the pit and the cyclist had been in plain view but unseen.

qa.q: What new rule did Zainab make, and why does it help?
qa.a: The phone stays in the bag until inside the gate, because glances at the road while texting are not enough for attention to catch a pit or a cyclist.

qa.q: What might the fruit-seller uncle have seen from the stall?
qa.a: He probably saw someone walking straight toward the pit with eyes on a phone, and grabbed an arm because there was no time to shout.

grounding: Shows a teenager texting while walking who looks at the road but fails to see an open pit and a cyclist.

passage:
Karthik: reached home. hands still shaking
Madhuri: what happened??
Karthik: near the Christmas market on Brigade Road. I was on a call with Sid about the party and following the map
Karthik: an old man was right on the zebra crossing. red sweater. I was looking straight at the crossing and didn't SEE him
Madhuri: 😰 did you hit him
Karthik: no. braked about a metre away. he banged on the bonnet, fair enough
Madhuri: so glad you're both ok
Karthik: I always thought only careless people do this. I'm not careless
Madhuri: it's not about being careless. your brain was on the call
Karthik: yeah. phone goes on drive mode from tomorrow. calls wait. map set before I start
Madhuri: 👍 and pull over if anything's urgent

qa.q: What was the old man wearing?
qa.a: A red sweater.

qa.q: Why is Karthik so shaken by what happened?
qa.a: He is frightened because he looked straight at the crossing and still didn't see the man, which upsets his belief that only careless people do this.

qa.q: What could Karthik do to guard his attention while driving?
qa.a: Put the phone on drive mode, let calls wait, set the map before starting, and pull over if something is urgent.

qa.q: How might the old man have felt on the zebra crossing?
qa.a: He was probably terrified and angry, which is why he banged on the bonnet after the car stopped so close.

grounding: Shows a young driver on a call who misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention rather than a flaw of character.

passage:
I've worked beside Ganga on the plant's maintenance crew for a year, and I've noticed something the rest of us used to laugh at. Before every lockout check on the big press, she puts her phone in her locker. Not her pocket, the locker.
Once, when her brother called three times during a check, I saw it buzzing on the shelf as we walked past. She kept going through the tags, one, two, three, reading each out loud.
After any electrical job she waves someone over. "Aparna, second pair of eyes?" We go through her checklist together, even when she's sure.
In June the new supervisor rushed a job and skipped the second check. A breaker was left live. Nobody was hurt, only because Ganga, walking past, stopped and looked.
I can't say what goes on in her head. But my phone lives in my locker now too.

qa.q: Where does Ganga put her phone before every lockout check?
qa.a: In her locker.

qa.q: Why might Ganga ask for a second pair of eyes even when she is sure?
qa.a: She seems to trust the check more than her own certainty and feels calm rather than embarrassed about being checked, since one missed detail could be dangerous.

qa.q: What went wrong in June, and what would have prevented it?
qa.a: The new supervisor rushed a job and skipped the second check, leaving a breaker live; a second person going through the checklist would likely have caught it.

qa.q: How has Ganga's habit changed Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna, who used to laugh along, now keeps the phone in the locker too.

grounding: Shows a worker who keeps her phone away during safety checks and double-checks critical work with a second person.

passage:
It was the last night of the summer holidays, and Tejas still had two pages of holiday homework left. The cartoon channel was on, and his notebook was on his knees.
"I can do both," he told his elder brother Sachin. "I'm fast."
Sachin set a timer on his phone. For forty minutes Tejas wrote a sum, laughed at the screen, wrote half a sum, looked up again. When the timer rang, he had finished six sums, and three were wrong.
"Deal," said Sachin, switching off the TV. "Twenty minutes, TV off. Then you can watch the rest."
Tejas groaned. In twenty minutes he finished the second page, eight sums, all correct. He stared at the notebook. "That's weird."

qa.q: How many sums had Tejas finished when the timer rang?
qa.a: He had finished six sums, and three were wrong.

qa.q: Why does Tejas believe he can do both?
qa.a: He feels confident because he is fast, and switching quickly between the cartoon and the sums feels like doing both at once.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Twenty minutes with the TV off worked, because Tejas stopped switching and finished eight correct sums.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the timer experiment?
qa.a: Sachin likely wanted Tejas to see the difference himself instead of being told, and may feel quietly pleased when Tejas says "That's weird."

grounding: Shows a child who thinks he is doing homework and watching cartoons well at the same time, while switching makes each slower and worse.

passage:
During the Pongal holidays Saurabh studied on the thinnai of their house in the small town, textbook on one side, phone on the other. Every few minutes it pinged: the class group planning the kite contest, Lavanya asking which colour string to buy, a cousin's jokes.
He answered each one in seconds and went back to the page. He felt busy and quick, as if he was getting through everything.
But each time he looked back at the trigonometry chapter, he had to read the last paragraph again to find his place. After an hour he was still on the same two pages.
Lavanya cycled past his gate and called, "How much did you finish?"
"Loads," he said. Then he looked down. "Two pages."

qa.q: Which chapter was Saurabh studying?
qa.a: The trigonometry chapter.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel productive while replying to messages?
qa.a: Answering each ping in seconds made him feel busy and quick, so he didn't notice the time he lost finding his place again.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try in the next study hour?
qa.a: He could leave the phone inside the house for a set time, then answer the kite group and Lavanya all at once in a break.

qa.q: What might Lavanya think when Saurabh says "Two pages"?
qa.a: She might be surprised or amused, since his quick replies all hour made it seem he was studying a lot.

grounding: Shows a teenager replying to messages while studying who feels productive but loses focus with each switch.

Pema: Swati, quick q. in today's hour-long meeting, did you catch the launch date change?
Swati: wait, there was a change?
Pema: yep. moved to the 14th. I said it twice
Swati: oh no 😬 I was fixing a report during the meeting
Pema: not blaming you. I counted, 6 of 8 people were typing the whole time. I did the same last week
Swati: honestly the meetings are so long it feels wasteful to just sit
Pema: that's the loop. long meetings, people half-listen, we repeat things, meetings get longer
Pema: trying something from Monday: 20 minutes max, laptops closed, one notes-taker. you all get 40 minutes back
Swati: closed laptops feels scary lol. but ok, I'm in 👍

qa.q: What is the new launch date?
qa.a: The 14th.

qa.q: What might Pema be feeling after counting six of eight people typing?
qa.a: Pema seems concerned but not angry, admitting to doing the same last week and wanting to fix the pattern rather than blame anyone.

qa.q: What norm is Pema setting, and why could it work?
qa.a: Twenty-minute meetings with laptops closed and one notes-taker, because full attention for a short time replaces long, half-heard meetings.

qa.q: How does Swati feel about closing laptops?
qa.a: Swati finds it a little scary, since sitting without working seemed wasteful, but agrees to try.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing colleagues half-listening while typing and setting a norm of short meetings with full attention.

passage:
On a noisy bus home after the Christmas holidays, Thomas told Gargi Aunty about the zoo. "We saw a lion. It was sleeping."
At the next stop he told it again, louder over the horns. "The lion ROARED at me!"
By the third stop, hugging his new lion book, he was bouncing. "The lion jumped out of the cage, and Papa fought it with a stick, like in my book!"
Mummy smiled at Gargi Aunty and whispered, "It slept the whole time."
Thomas nodded hard. "It jumped. I saw it."

qa.q: What was Thomas hugging at the third stop?
qa.a: His new lion book.

qa.q: Why does Thomas insist "I saw it"?
qa.a: Each time he tells it, bits from his lion book slip into the memory, so he feels sure and excited that the lion really jumped.

qa.q: How could Mummy gently help Thomas with the story?
qa.a: She could enjoy it with him and ask, "In your book the lion jumps. At the zoo, what was the lion doing?", without calling it a lie.

qa.q: What might Gargi Aunty think as the story grows at each stop?
qa.a: She probably finds it sweet and funny, watching a sleeping lion turn into a fight, especially after Mummy's whisper.

grounding: Shows a preschooler whose retelling of a zoo visit takes in details from a storybook until he believes the new version.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, first week after the Puja holidays
In our holiday stories circle, Chetan described his family's trip to Darjeeling in detail: the toy train, the fog, and a monkey that stole his elder sister Rimi's sandwich on the platform.
At pickup his mother laughed: the monkey story belongs to Rimi's school trip two years ago. Chetan wasn't there. When I asked Chetan gently, he looked puzzled, then certain. "No, I saw it! It had a white face."
He wasn't lying. He had heard Rimi tell it so often that it had become part of his own trip.
The next day we did a class activity: two children describe the same event, and we notice the differences without calling anyone wrong. Chetan loved it.
Afreen Ma'am

qa.q: What did Chetan say the monkey stole?
qa.a: His elder sister Rimi's sandwich, on the platform.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel when he was asked gently about the monkey?
qa.a: He was puzzled at first, then certain and a little indignant, because the story felt like a real memory of his own.

qa.q: Why was the class activity a good response?
qa.a: It showed that memories of the same event differ without calling anyone a liar, so Chetan could learn without feeling ashamed.

qa.q: How might Rimi feel hearing her monkey story in Chetan's trip?
qa.a: Rimi might be amused or a bit annoyed that her story has been borrowed, though Chetan truly believes it.

grounding: Shows a child retelling a family trip with a sibling's story mixed in and believing it fully.
